Chapter 4: The Emotional and Physical Toll of Racism on All Americans
Picture this: It’s still dark outside, and a nurse is getting ready for another long shift at the hospital. She knows what’s ahead—too many patients, not enough help, and this constant push to do more with less. But what she might not realize is that the stress she feels isn’t just about the job. It’s connected to bigger forces—forces that shape not only her work, but the health of the whole community.
You know, we often think of racism as a problem that only hurts the people who are targeted by it. But here’s something important: the truth is a lot more complicated. The systems and beliefs that separate people by race don’t just harm some—they create stress, anxiety, and even illness for everyone. That nurse sees it every day in her patients. High blood pressure, depression, chronic pain—these are more common in communities that have been pushed to the margins. But she also feels it personally, in the exhaustion of working in a system that’s always under pressure.
The physical toll of racism? It’s real, and it’s well-documented. When people are denied good jobs, safe homes, or decent healthcare, they’re more likely to get sick or die early. But it doesn’t stop there. Even folks who seem to benefit from these systems—maybe because of their status or privilege—end up paying a price. There’s the constant pressure to keep up, the fear of losing what they have, and the isolation that comes from living in a divided world. All of that chips away at their mental and physical well-being.
Think about a manager who’s always worried about being seen as “soft” or “weak.” He pushes himself to the edge, ignoring all the signs that he’s burning out. Or a child who’s taught to fear people who are different—growing up anxious, suspicious, never really trusting anyone. These aren’t just personal struggles. They’re the result of a society that values competition over cooperation, exclusion over inclusion.
The stress of living in a divided society isn’t shared equally, but it does touch everyone. When we’re taught to view each other as threats, community breaks down. Trust becomes rare, and the support everyone needs just fades away. The end result? A society where loneliness, fear, and illness are common—even for those who seem to have every advantage.
Most people don’t see how these problems are connected to the bigger systems shaping their lives. They blame themselves for feeling tired, anxious, or disconnected. But here’s the thing: a lot of these feelings come from living in a world built around exclusion and competition. The costs of racism aren’t just carried by those who are targeted—they’re shared by everyone.
And yet, even with all these challenges, there are moments of real hope. Maybe a team at work decides to support each other through a tough project, choosing cooperation over competition. Or a family finds new ways to connect, breaking old habits of fear and suspicion. These moments remind us—the emotional and physical toll of racism isn’t set in stone. It can be faced, and it can be changed.
The first step toward healing is noticing how systems of exclusion shape our daily lives. When we start connecting our personal struggles to these bigger social forces, we can imagine new ways of living together. A healthier, more connected society—it’s not just a dream. It’s something we can work toward, starting right now.
